steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for an ML paper proposing a self-supervised representation learning method that learns from random data projectors instead of data augmentations. Explain the limits of augmentation-based and masking-based self-supervised learning, motivate and formally sketch our approach, and summarize what the experiments show.

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Self-supervised learning and transformation invariance
  - SSRL associated with well-designed pretext tasks; heuristics to encode useful info from unlabelled data
  - pretext tasks customized per application but based on a handful of assumptions
  - transformation invariance across augmentation views: leading performance in several domains
  - vision: representation unchanged after cropping, rotating, flipping, corrupting
  - NLP: sentences with similar words/semantic meaning -> same representation
  - enforced via contrastive or momentum objectives
- Augmentations are tied to modalities
  - SSRL with transformation invariance does not support generic data types
  - augmentations tailored to specific modalities; limited generality across domains
  - e.g. Gaussian noise not directly applicable to text; image rotation not applicable to tabular
  - -> augmentation-based SSRL constrained in cross-domain applicability
- Augmentations can conflict with application constraints
  - pathology images of stained tissue: low color variation -> naive color-jittering unnatural (Fig. 1)
  - such images inappropriate/unsafe for critical medical imaging
  - time series with high periodicity (online monitoring): random shifting -> identical augmented views, useless for pretext tasks
  - tabular: few augmentation options; random noise or feature swapping -> unrealistic examples
  - particle physics: energies and momenta of interacting particles; physics constrains combinations; tabular augmentations -> unphysical, inconsistent representations, unpredictable downstream failures
- Masking-based alternatives
  - masking and reconstructing input: masked image modelling (vision), masked language modelling (NLP)
  - often need specific backbones like transformers for good performance
- Learning from randomness (LFR)
  - SSRL scheme without domain-specific augmentations or particular architectures
  - hypothesis: good representations from learning to reconstruct multiple randomly generated data projection functions
  - motivation: representation learning captures abstract, valuable concepts supporting a range of downstream tasks; these could include arbitrary data projections
  - formal: G=\{\cdots g^{(k)}(\mathbf{x})\cdots\}, inputs \mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}; good \mathbf{z} -> simple predictors H=\{\cdots h^{(k)}(\mathbf{z})\cdots\}
  - search for \mathbf{z} and H reproducing random projections
- Advantages and results
  - random projections easy to create for any modality: randomly initialized network suited to the data
  - applies to all subfields of SSRL; no augmentations -> no unsafe, identical, unrealistic augmentations
  - evaluated on image, sequential, tabular data; banking, healthcare, natural sciences
  - outperforms common domain-agnostic SSRL; competitive with many domain-specific approaches
  - learning from randomness feasible alternative when transformation invariance hard to establish/enforce

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Learning data representations in a self-supervised way is usually associated with well-designed pretext tasks, which create heuristics so that machine learning models can identify and encode useful information from unlabelled data. Pretext tasks are often very customized to specific applications, but they are typically based on a handful of underlying assumptions. Pretext tasks that use the transformation invariance assumption across data augmentation views show leading performance in several research domains. In computer vision, image representations are usually guided to stay the same after cropping, rotating, flipping, or corrupting, and so on. In the same way, in natural language processing, sentences with similar words and semantic meaning are expected to have the same representation. In these domains and others, transformation invariance is encouraged explicitly with contrastive or momentum objectives that try to bring representations before and after the transformation together.

Self-supervised representation learning (SSRL) algorithms that enforce transformation invariance perform strongly in many domains, but they are limited because they do not support generic data types. Many well-known data augmentation methods are made for specific modalities, and their generality across different domains is restricted. For instance, Gaussian noise corruption can't be applied directly to textual data, and image rotation is not applicable in the tabular domain. So augmentation based SSRL techniques are inherently constrained in how well they apply across domains.

These examples show limitations with modalities, but there is a more subtle problem, which is that even standard augmentations can conflict with constraints that are specific to the application. For example, pathology images of stained tissue samples have low color variation, so naïve color-jittering produces augmentations that are unnatural (see Fig. 1). Incorrect images like this may be inappropriate and unsafe to use in critical medical imaging applications. For time series that have high periodicity, such as online monitoring data, random shifting augmentations can create identical augmented views, which are not useful for pretext tasks. In tabular settings there are relatively few options for augmentations, and random noise addition or randomly swapping features between training examples can easily produce examples that are unrealistic. A concrete example is from particle physics, where energies and momenta of interacting particles are collected experimentally. The incoming and outgoing energies are constrained by the laws of physics, so only certain combinations can be observed. Tabular augmentations would produce combinations that are unphysical, and this harms the consistency of the learned representations and leads to failures on downstream tasks that are unpredictable.

- Masking-based alternatives
  - masking and reconstructing input: masked image modelling (vision), masked language modelling (NLP)
  - often need specific backbones like transformers for good performance
- Learning from randomness (LFR)
  - SSRL scheme without domain-specific augmentations or particular architectures
  - hypothesis: good representations from learning to reconstruct multiple randomly generated data projection functions
  - motivation: representation learning captures abstract, valuable concepts supporting a range of downstream tasks; these could include arbitrary data projections
  - formal: G=\{\cdots g^{(k)}(\mathbf{x})\cdots\}, inputs \mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}; good \mathbf{z} -> simple predictors H=\{\cdots h^{(k)}(\mathbf{z})\cdots\}
  - search for \mathbf{z} and H reproducing random projections
- Advantages and results
  - random projections easy to create for any modality: randomly initialized network suited to the data
  - applies to all subfields of SSRL; no augmentations -> no unsafe, identical, unrealistic augmentations
  - evaluated on image, sequential, tabular data; banking, healthcare, natural sciences
  - outperforms common domain-agnostic SSRL; competitive with many domain-specific approaches
  - learning from randomness feasible alternative when transformation invariance hard to establish/enforce

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Learning data representations in a self-supervised way is usually associated with well-designed pretext tasks, which create heuristics so that machine learning models can identify and encode useful information from unlabelled data. Pretext tasks are often very customized to specific applications, but they are typically based on a handful of underlying assumptions. Pretext tasks that use the transformation invariance assumption across data augmentation views show leading performance in several research domains. In computer vision, image representations are usually guided to stay the same after cropping, rotating, flipping, or corrupting, and so on. In the same way, in natural language processing, sentences with similar words and semantic meaning are expected to have the same representation. In these domains and others, transformation invariance is encouraged explicitly with contrastive or momentum objectives that try to bring representations before and after the transformation together.

Self-supervised representation learning (SSRL) algorithms that enforce transformation invariance perform strongly in many domains, but they are limited because they do not support generic data types. Many well-known data augmentation methods are made for specific modalities, and their generality across different domains is restricted. For instance, Gaussian noise corruption can't be applied directly to textual data, and image rotation is not applicable in the tabular domain. So augmentation based SSRL techniques are inherently constrained in how well they apply across domains.

These examples show limitations with modalities, but there is a more subtle problem, which is that even standard augmentations can conflict with constraints that are specific to the application. For example, pathology images of stained tissue samples have low color variation, so naïve color-jittering produces augmentations that are unnatural (see Fig. 1). Incorrect images like this may be inappropriate and unsafe to use in critical medical imaging applications. For time series that have high periodicity, such as online monitoring data, random shifting augmentations can create identical augmented views, which are not useful for pretext tasks. In tabular settings there are relatively few options for augmentations, and random noise addition or randomly swapping features between training examples can easily produce examples that are unrealistic. A concrete example is from particle physics, where energies and momenta of interacting particles are collected experimentally. The incoming and outgoing energies are constrained by the laws of physics, so only certain combinations can be observed. Tabular augmentations would produce combinations that are unphysical, and this harms the consistency of the learned representations and leads to failures on downstream tasks that are unpredictable.

Instead of transformation invariance, many self-supervised learning techniques mask and reconstruct the input data, including masked image modelling for computer vision and masked language modelling for natural language processing. However, these methods often need specific backbone architectures like transformers to get good performance.

In this paper we introduce a SSRL training scheme that needs neither domain-specific data augmentations nor particular architectures like the masking approaches. Instead, the learning method is based on a surprising hypothesis, which is that good data representations can be obtained by learning to reconstruct multiple randomly generated data projection functions at the same time. The hypothesis comes from the conventional motivation of representation learning, which is to capture and extract abstract and valuable concepts that can support a range of downstream predictive tasks. In particular, these downstream tasks could include arbitrary data projections. Formally, if we have random projection functions G=\{\cdots g^{(k)}(\mathbf{x})\cdots\} whose input domains are raw data features \mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}, the motivation above suggests that for a good representation \mathbf{z} of data \mathbf{x}, there is another group of simple prediction functions H=\{\cdots h^{(k)}(\mathbf{z})\cdots\} that can predict the outputs of the random functions correctly. So the representation learning task can be seen as a search for a combination of representation \mathbf{z} and prediction functions H that can reproduce random data projections. In short, we do SSRL by learning from randomness (LFR).

The main advantage of LFR is that random projection functions G are easy to create for any data modality. One straightforward way is to take a neural network with a suitable architecture for the data and initialize its parameters randomly. So LFR applies to all subfields of SSRL. Also, LFR does not use data augmentations, so it avoids the concerns about unsafe, identical, or unrealistic augmentations that we discussed above.

We evaluate LFR empirically on many representation learning tasks that cover diverse data types (including image, sequential, and tabular) and multiple real-world applications (banking, healthcare and natural sciences). The results show that LFR outperforms domain-agnostic SSRL algorithms that are commonly used. It is even competitive with many domain-specific approaches that depend heavily on expert knowledge for designing their data augmentations. This performance shows that learning high-quality data representations from randomness is a feasible and plausible alternative when the transformation invariance assumption is hard to establish or enforce in an application domain.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Learning data representations in a self-supervised manner is commonly associated with well-designed pretext tasks that create heuristics for machine learning models to identify and encode useful information from unlabelled data. While pretext tasks are often highly customized to specific applications, they are typically based on a handful of underlying assumptions. Pretext tasks utilizing the transformation invariance assumption across data augmentation views show leading performance in multiple research domains. For computer vision, image representations are commonly guided to remain identical after cropping, rotating, flipping, or corrupting, among others [1,2]. Similarly, in natural language processing, sentences with similar words and semantic meaning are expected to have the same representation [3,4]. In these and other domains, transformation invariance is encouraged explicitly through contrastive or momentum objectives that aim to bring together representations before and after transformation.

Despite their strong performance in many domains, self-supervised representation learning (SSRL) algorithms that enforce transformation invariance are limited in that they do not support generic data types. Many well-known data augmentation methods are tailored to specific modalities and are restricted in their generality across domains. For instance, Gaussian noise corruption cannot be applied directly to textual data, while image rotation is not applicable in the tabular domain. Thus, augmentation-based SSRL techniques are inherently constrained in their cross-domain applicability.

Beyond these modality limitations, a more subtle problem is that even standard augmentations can conflict with application-specific constraints. For example, pathology images of stained tissue samples have low color variation [5,6], so naïve color-jittering produces unnatural augmentations (see Fig. 1). Such incorrect images may be inappropriate and unsafe for use in critical medical imaging applications [7]. For time series with high periodicity, such as online monitoring data, random shifting augmentations can create identical augmented views that are not useful for pretext tasks [10,11]. In tabular settings, where relatively few augmentation options are available, random noise addition or random swapping of features between training examples can easily produce unrealistic examples. As a concrete example from particle physics, consider energies and momenta of interacting particles collected experimentally [12]. Since the incoming and outgoing energies are constrained by the laws of physics, only certain combinations can be observed. Tabular augmentations would produce unphysical combinations, harming the consistency of learned representations and leading to unpredictable failures on downstream tasks [13].

Instead of relying on transformation invariance, many self-supervised learning techniques mask and reconstruct input data, including masked image modelling [14,15] for computer vision and masked language modelling [16,17] for natural language processing. However, these methods often require specific backbone architectures such as transformers [18] to achieve good performance [19].

In this paper, we introduce a SSRL training scheme that requires neither domain-specific data augmentations nor particular architectures as in masking approaches. Instead, the proposed learning method is based on a surprising hypothesis: good data representations can be obtained by learning to simultaneously reconstruct multiple randomly generated data projection functions. The hypothesis comes from the conventional motivation of representation learning, namely capturing and extracting abstract and valuable concepts that can support a range of downstream predictive tasks [20,21]. In particular, these downstream tasks could include arbitrary data projections. Formally, given random projection functions G=\{\cdots g^{(k)}(\mathbf{x})\cdots\} whose input domains are raw data features \mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}, the motivation above suggests that, for a good representation \mathbf{z} of data \mathbf{x}, there is another group of simple prediction functions H=\{\cdots h^{(k)}(\mathbf{z})\cdots\} that can correctly predict the random functions' outputs. Seen this way, the representation learning task becomes a search for a combination of representation \mathbf{z} and prediction functions H that can reproduce random data projections. In short, we conduct SSRL by learning from randomness (LFR).

The primary advantage of LFR is that random projection functions G can easily be created for any data modality. One straightforward instantiation is to take a neural network with an architecture suitable for consuming the data and randomly initialize its parameters. Hence, LFR applies to all subfields of SSRL. Also, since data augmentations are not used, LFR avoids the concerns about unsafe, identical, or unrealistic augmentations discussed above.

We empirically evaluate the effectiveness of LFR on a wide range of representation learning tasks spanning diverse data types (including image, sequential, and tabular) and multiple real-world applications (banking, healthcare and natural sciences). The results show that LFR outperforms commonly used domain-agnostic SSRL algorithms, and is even competitive with many domain-specific approaches that rely heavily on expert knowledge for their data augmentation designs. This performance demonstrates that learning high-quality data representations from randomness is a feasible and plausible alternative when the transformation invariance assumption is hard to establish or enforce in a given application domain.
